title: Footprints: The Book That Saved the Earth

topics.title: A science-fiction play: word roots of the future

learn.hook: Martians plan to invade Earth, and are stopped by a book of nursery rhymes!
points: 'The Book That Saved the Earth' by Claire Boiko is a science-fiction play introduced by a historian from the 25th century.
From Mars, the proud leader Think-Tank and his apprentice Noodle guide a crew (Captain Omega, Lieutenant Iota and Sergeant Oop) who land on Earth, enter a library and try to understand its books.
Reading a book of Mother Goose nursery rhymes, they take the silly verses as secret warnings, panic and call off the invasion.
Science fiction imagines future science, space travel and other worlds; it often comments on our own world.
Science words often use Greek or Latin roots: tele- (far), micro- (small), astro- (star), bio- (life), -scope (instrument for viewing).

example.q: Think it through: What do 'telescope' and 'microscope' mean, using their roots?
steps: tele- means far; micro- means small.
-scope means an instrument for viewing.
So a telescope views far things and a microscope views very small things.
example.answer: Telescope: an instrument to see distant things; microscope: an instrument to see very small things.

learn.reallife: ISRO's missions, like Chandrayaan and Mangalyaan, show how yesterday's science fiction becomes today's science.

games.title: Sci-fi play check
items: The leader of the Martians is called Think-Tank.
Think-Tank is the proud Martian leader.
The Martians are stopped by Earth's army.
They are 'stopped' by a book of nursery rhymes.
The play is introduced by a historian from the 25th century.
The historian looks back at the 'Age of the Book'.
Science fiction is always set in the past.
It usually imagines the future or other worlds.
'Astronaut' contains the root astro-, meaning star.
Astro- comes from the Greek word for star.

quiz.q: Who is the leader of the Martians in 'The Book That Saved the Earth'?
quiz.explain: Think-Tank is the Martians' proud leader.
steps: The Martians in the play are led by a proud leader.
His name is Think-Tank (Noodle is his apprentice).
Answer: Think-Tank
quiz.mistake: Confuses the leader with his apprentice

quiz.q: Which book 'saves the Earth' in the play?
options: A book of Mother Goose nursery rhymes
quiz.explain: The Martians misread nursery rhymes as threats.
steps: The book the Martians find is a book of nursery rhymes.
Their misreading of Mother Goose rhymes saves the Earth.
Answer: A book of Mother Goose nursery rhymes
quiz.mistake: Assumes a serious book must have saved the Earth

quiz.q: Why does Think-Tank call off the invasion?
options: He misreads the nursery rhymes as signs of danger
quiz.explain: He takes harmless rhymes as secret warnings and panics.
steps: Think-Tank takes the harmless rhymes as secret warnings of Earth's power.
He panics and calls off the invasion.
Answer: He misreads the nursery rhymes as signs of danger

quiz.explain: A historian from the future introduces and frames the story.
steps: The play is framed by a speaker from the future.
A historian from the 25th century introduces it.
Answer: A historian from the 25th century
quiz.mistake: Confuses the narrator with a character

quiz.q: Which is a feature of science fiction?
options: It imagines future science, space travel or other worlds
It is always a true story
It is only about kings and queens
quiz.explain: Sci-fi is built on imagined science and technology.
steps: Science fiction is built on imagined science and technology.
It imagines future science, space travel or other worlds.
Answer: It imagines future science, space travel or other worlds
quiz.mistake: Confuses sci-fi with history or fairy tales

quiz.explain: Telephone, television, telescope: all about distance.
steps: Think of telephone, television, telescope.
They all involve distance, so 'tele-' means far.
Answer: far
Think of microscope and microchip.
They are about very small things, so 'micro-' means small.
Answer: small

quiz.explain: astro- means star and -naut means sailor: a 'star sailor'.
steps: astro- means star and -naut means sailor.
So astronaut literally suggests a star sailor.
Answer: A star sailor
quiz.mistake: Does not break the word into its parts

teach.ask: Gappu: How can a book of baby rhymes stop an alien invasion? And what is science fiction?
teach.praise: Beep-chirp! The Martians misunderstood the rhymes and ran away. Sci-fi with a giggle!
teach.nudge: What did the Martians read, and did they understand it correctly?

revise.summary: 'The Book That Saved the Earth' by Claire Boiko is a science-fiction play, introduced by a 25th-century historian, in which Martians misread Mother Goose nursery rhymes as warnings and call off their invasion. We also learn Greek and Latin word roots.
focus: Know the characters: Think-Tank (leader), Noodle (apprentice), and the crew.
Explain why the invasion is called off.
Use word roots to work out meanings.
remember: Science fiction imagines future science, space travel and other worlds; it often comments on our own world.
tele- (far), micro- (small), astro- (star), bio- (life), -scope (instrument for viewing).
traps: Don't confuse the leader Think-Tank with his apprentice Noodle.
No battle took place; the Martians panicked over nursery rhymes.
Don't mix up tele- (far) and micro- (small).

topics.title: Humour in the play: misunderstandings, puns and homophones

learn.hook: A mighty Martian leader frightened by an egg sitting on a wall: comedy at its best!
points: The play's humour comes from misunderstanding: the Martians read simple nursery rhymes as serious codes.
Think-Tank is conceited (too proud of himself) and insults his apprentice Noodle, yet he is the one who is fooled.
Dramatic irony: the audience knows the rhymes are harmless, but the Martians are terrified.
A pun plays on two meanings of a word, or on words that sound alike: 'The book on anti-gravity is impossible to put down.'
Homophones sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning: read/reed, their/there, knight/night, write/right.

example.q: Why is it funny that Think-Tank, who thinks he is brilliant, is scared off by a nursery rhyme?
steps: He boasts of his great mind and mocks Noodle.
Yet he cannot understand simple children's verses.
The proud one being fooled by something harmless is ironic and comic.
example.answer: His pride makes the misunderstanding funnier: the 'genius' is beaten by a children's rhyme.

learn.reallife: Comedy films and TV shows often use mix-ups and wordplay, like a character mishearing 'desert' as 'dessert'.

games.title: Make a sentence
games.prompt: Arrange the words to make a sentence

quiz.q: What mainly makes 'The Book That Saved the Earth' funny?
options: The Martians seriously misunderstand simple nursery rhymes
quiz.explain: Their serious misreading of silly rhymes creates the comedy.
steps: The Martians treat simple nursery rhymes as serious threats.
Their serious misunderstanding is what makes the play funny.
Answer: The Martians seriously misunderstand simple nursery rhymes
quiz.mistake: Thinks the humour comes from jokes told by characters

quiz.explain: He is very proud of his own mind and keeps insulting Noodle.
steps: Think-Tank is very proud of his own mind and insults Noodle.
That makes him conceited.
Answer: Conceited
quiz.mistake: Takes his high opinion of himself as true

quiz.explain: Noodle is the apprentice whom Think-Tank keeps insulting.
steps: Think-Tank's assistant, whom he keeps insulting, is Noodle.
So Noodle is the apprentice.
Answer: Noodle

quiz.q: The audience knows the rhymes are harmless, but the Martians are terrified. What is this?
quiz.explain: The audience knows something the characters do not.
steps: The audience knows the rhymes are harmless; the characters do not.
When the audience knows more than the characters, it is dramatic irony.
Answer: Dramatic irony
quiz.mistake: Confuses dramatic irony with other devices

options: A play on words using two meanings or similar sounds
quiz.explain: Puns are jokes based on words with double meanings.
steps: A pun is a joke on words.
It plays on two meanings or similar sounds of a word.
Answer: A play on words using two meanings or similar sounds
quiz.mistake: Confuses pun with simile or alliteration

options: I'm reading a long book about space.
I'm reading a book on anti-gravity; it's impossible to put down.
The book is on the table.
quiz.explain: 'Impossible to put down' means both 'very interesting' and 'it floats'.
steps: A pun uses a phrase with two meanings.
'Impossible to put down' means both 'very interesting' and 'it floats away' (anti-gravity).
Answer: I'm reading a book on anti-gravity; it's impossible to put down.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the double meaning

quiz.q: Choose the right word: 'The Martians landed ___, near the library.'
quiz.explain: 'There' shows a place; 'their' shows possession; 'they're' = they are.
steps: 'There' shows a place; 'their' shows possession; 'they're' means they are.
Landing near the library is a place, so 'there'.
Answer: there

options: Words that sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning
steps: Homophones sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning.
Examples: read/reed, knight/night.
Answer: Words that sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning
quiz.mistake: Confuses homophones with synonyms or antonyms

teach.ask: Gappu: Why do people laugh when Think-Tank gets scared? And what are those words that sound the same, like 'night' and 'knight'?
teach.praise: Ha-chirp! The proud leader misunderstands a silly rhyme, and 'night' and 'knight' are homophones. Comedy cracked!
teach.nudge: Why is a proud leader being fooled funny? What do we call words that sound the same but mean different things?

revise.summary: The play is funny because the conceited Think-Tank and his Martians take harmless nursery rhymes as serious codes, while the audience knows better. We also learn dramatic irony, puns and homophones.
focus: Explain where the humour comes from: misunderstanding and dramatic irony.
Identify puns and choose the right homophone.
remember: Dramatic irony: the audience knows the rhymes are harmless, but the Martians are terrified.
A pun plays on two meanings of a word, or on words that sound alike.
Homophones sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning: read/reed, their/there, knight/night, write/right.
traps: Don't take Think-Tank's high opinion of himself as true.
Homophones are not synonyms or antonyms.
